page.title: tinyactors compared with Temporal
page.description: Where a workflow with retries and timeouts runs, how its tests move time, what a crash keeps, and when Temporal is the better choice.

hero.headline: Retries and timeouts, without a Temporal server
hero.lede: A payment that retries every 30 seconds runs as a statechart inside your Node.js or Python process. One program checks it over a thousand simulated runs, with no server and no database. Choose Temporal when its service must keep every workflow through a machine's failure.

section.heading: Temporal is a service; tinyactors is a library
section.p: A payment that retries three times is a few states of logic. With Temporal, it spans a server, a database and the workers you run. tinyactors keeps it in your process.

claim.statement: Temporal runs a server and its database
claim.p: Its docs define the service as the Temporal Server combined with persistence and visibility stores.
In production the store is Cassandra, PostgreSQL or MySQL. SQLite is for development and testing only.

claim.statement: Your workers poll the service for tasks
claim.p: Worker processes are external to the service, and you operate them. Each one polls a task queue, runs your code and reports the result back.

claim.statement: A tinyactors host lives in your program
claim.p: new Host(charts, options) runs the actors inside the program that imports @tinyactors/node or tinyactors. A chart reaches the world only through handlers you give the host.
claim.source: Home, "The chart decides, your code acts"
I/O processors, "Ask for outside work with a send"

section.p: Temporal Cloud takes the service off your hands: Temporal operates its persistence, replication, upgrades and availability. Your workers still run in your environment (Temporal, "Temporal Cloud").

section.heading: Test a thousand payments in one program
section.p: A workflow's bugs hide in its timeouts. This chart charges a card, charges again after 30 seconds without an answer and gives up after three charges:

The test gives the host a stand-in payment service that answers 40% of charges. It moves a simulated clock straight to each timeout, so a run that would wait 90 seconds ends as soon as the chart is done. Then it checks two rules:

claim.statement: Temporal's tests skip time with a server
claim.p: Temporal's test framework is an in-memory Temporal Server whose timers fast-forward, except while activities run. The @temporalio/testing package downloads that server.

section.p: Here the host and its clock are the whole test. No server starts.
The stand-in service is an object, so it answers, fails or stays silent as each case needs ().

section.heading: Temporal keeps history; your program keeps snapshots
section.p: A process dies halfway through a payment. What survives depends on who wrote it down.

claim.statement: Temporal replays every workflow from its history
claim.p: The service records each workflow's event history, a complete ordered log that is its source of truth. To continue a workflow, it reruns the code from the beginning against that history.
Its docs say workflows keep running for years, even if the underlying infrastructure fails.

claim.statement: A crash keeps what your program saved
claim.p: tinyactors actors live in your process's memory, so a crash stops them all. What comes back is what your program saved: hibernated actors in its store, and its last snapshot.
Inputs after that snapshot return only if your program journaled them and replays them on the restored host.
claim.source: When to use tinyactors, "A crash stops memory and keeps saved state"
Snapshots, "Replay the inputs that came after"

section.p: So if no input may be lost and you'd rather not write that journal, choose Temporal.
A snapshot holds only its moment. A snapshot of two million actors takes 165 MB ().

section.heading: Change a workflow that is already running
section.p: An order waits a week for delivery. On Tuesday the rules change. The running order must take the new rules without losing its place.

claim.statement: Temporal's replay needs deterministic code and patches
claim.p: Replay reruns workflow code, so given the same input it must make the same API calls in the same order. Adding, removing or reordering one causes a nondeterminism error.
patched() marks a change in the event history, a branch like a feature flag, so running workflows keep their old path.

claim.statement: A migration moves running actors to a version
claim.p: A new chart version is added to the running host, and host.migrate() moves running actors to it. Each keeps its active states, queue and delayed sends, and receives its old variables in an event.
claim.source: Migration, "Move the actors and carry their variables"

section.heading: Choose tinyactors for logic inside your program

item.term: Workflows in a program you already run
item.text: The host is a library, so no server, database or worker fleet runs beside your program.
A simulated clock jumps to each deadline, so one program checks a payment's rules over a thousand runs.

item.term: Many workflows, most of them waiting
item.text: Waiting actors hibernate into your store: two million ran with at most 1000 in memory, the rest in SQLite.
Every state and transition is in one SCXML chart, which a test, a reviewer or the command line can read.

section.heading: Choose Temporal when its service must own durability

item.text: The service keeps each workflow's event history in its database. Replay restores the state after infrastructure fails.
Workers on any machine poll task queues. tinyactors leaves placement and failover between hosts to your program.
Temporal retries a failed activity by default, starting after one second and doubling. In a chart, you write each retry as a transition.
A workflow is code in your language, with no chart format to learn (Temporal, "Workflow Definition").
